# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- adopt-claudinite: Bootstrap Claudinite into a consuming repo — mount, hooks, checks, skills. Use when asked to bootstrap, adopt, or set up Claudinite, or to baseline a repo to pick up updates.
- adopt-pack: Add one or more packs to an already-adopted Claudinite member — declare, run each pack's adoption interview, re-vendor, scaffold, land. Use when asked to adopt, add, enable, or declare a pack (e.g. product-wiki, executable-requirements) on a repo that already runs Claudinite.
- authoring-agent-docs: How to write instruction files coding agents follow reliably. Use before writing or editing any Claude instruction doc — a project CLAUDE.md, a convention doc, a routine spec.
- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- bump-version: Raise the project's version — a minor bump by default. Use when the owner says "bump version".
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and extract its working instructions into reusable canon packs plus the project's own local packs (.claudinite/local_packs/). Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. {"number":801,"title":"Migration to the work-item queue: two PRs, one same-day validation burst","body":"The phase plan for [tasks-dispatch DESIGN](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/docs/tasks-dispatch/DESIGN.md) (§14 points here). Design constraints from the owner (2026-08-13): **fewest disparate steps, fewest approval points, and certainty the same day** — we do not wait for a nightly run to learn whether the end state works. Deliberately generating real work (an engine release, pack updates, an extension release, research/extract material) to push traffic through every path is explicitly sanctioned.

**Approval points: two.** PR‑1 (mechanism + canon flip) and PR‑2 (fleet flip + slot deletion). Everything else is forcing and observing, which the mechanism itself defines as ordinary operations.

**What is already proven before step 1:** the simulator (`docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/`, in CI) rehearses every scenario in SCENARIOS.md, including the spec bugs it caught (F13, F14, the S28 stamped-wake precision). The coverage map in `sim/README.md` names exactly what only live traffic can prove — the burst below exists to cover precisely those rows.

Checkboxes track progress; each burst row's checkbox is checked only with an evidence URL (an issue showing the full lifecycle) appended beside it.

---

## Step 0 — rehearsal (done)

- [x] Simulator + scenario suite green in CI; coverage map names the live-only rows

## Step 1 — PR‑1 on canon: the whole mechanism, canon flipped (approval №1)

One PR containing everything, because the safety is the config flag and the disjoint issue families (`[claudinite-task]` vs `[claudinite-work]`), not PR granularity — rollback at any moment before Step 3 is a one-line config edit back to `"slots"`, with each mechanism's open items invisible to the other (proven: S29).

- [ ] Label vocabulary (`task:*`, `origin:schedule`, `outcome:*`) — create-if-missing wiring
- [ ] Tick workflow: cron at the hashed minute **plus `workflow_dispatch`** (the never-wait-for-the-cron lever the burst depends on)
- [ ] Executor workflow: post-tick drain + `labeled`-event runs, `required_secrets` and endpoint tokens stamped into its env (DESIGN §14 secrets path)
- [ ] Janitor re-target: executing-leash on the tick, agent leash, stale-ready, stuck-dependency sweep (F14)
- [ ] Dependency fields, the `after` pick-time yield, `create-work-item` + the wake/re-queue lever
- [ ] F8: signal collectors' self-trigger exclusions learn the new vocabulary **in this PR**, before any repo flips
- [ ] `taskScheduler.dispatch: "queue"` **on canon, in this same PR**; slot machinery stays in the tree, dormant on canon, live everywhere else
- [ ] Gate green: full suite (sim included) + conformance sweep
- [ ] **Approval №1: PR‑1 merged**

## Step 2 — the validation burst (same afternoon, zero approvals)

Fire the tick by `workflow_dispatch`, then drive **real work** through every live-only path. Each row's acceptance is an issue URL showing the full lifecycle on one item. Any row red = fix on canon (flag still reversible) and re-run that row — the burst is idempotent because forcing is idempotent.

- [ ] **B1 creation + first-item rule (S25):** dispatched tick creates every task's item `task:blocked` wearing its next anchor — the issue list is the dashboard
- [ ] **B2 the roll + reasons on record (S1′):** wake a task with no work (`tidy-issues` on a quiet morning): one ask, roll to tomorrow, reason visible
- [ ] **B3 agentic happy path + real CCR invocation + records (S2):** touch a stale issue, wake `tidy-issues`: claim comment → prework → hand-off → live session → `outcome:done` + exec record
- [ ] **B4 agentless path + `required_secrets` end to end (§14 secrets 1–4):** bump the extension version so `store-release` has a genuine release to ship; prework consumes the store token from the stamped env
- [ ] **B5 the chain + yield (S4/S23):** cut an engine release (real baselining work) and stage extract material; wake `baselining`, watch `growth-extract` yield then run the same hour
- [ ] **B6 hourly cadence (S22):** file a real extractor request, watch `create-extractor` catch it within the hour; otherwise its hourly roll is the evidence
- [ ] **B7 missing-secret posture + re-queue (§14 step 7, F7, S19):** point a scratch task at an endpoint whose secret is deliberately unset: hand-off converges `needs-human` naming it; set the secret, re-queue, watch it converge

1	# Task dispatch without slots — the work-item queue
2	
3	Status: **agreed in shape; not yet built.** A continuation of the owner's
4	sketch (2026-08-12, reproduced in Appendix A), played against twenty timed
5	scenarios ([SCENARIOS.md](SCENARIOS.md)) and the field's prior art
6	([RESEARCH.md](RESEARCH.md)), with the owner's eight decisions of 2026-08-13
7	recorded in §15 and folded into the sections they changed. The phase plan
8	belongs to a tracking issue, not here. It supersedes
9	the slot machinery of
10	[per-project-scheduling DESIGN §3–§5](../per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md) and
11	amends several of its §12 decisions (each amendment is named where it happens).
12	What it does **not** touch: the task folder anatomy (§1), the precondition
13	contract, prework and its secrets model
14	([task-prework DESIGN](../task-prework/DESIGN.md)), the outcome ceiling, the
15	security posture (the issue is data; behavior comes from tracked files), and the
16	usage-metrics records.
17	
18	The shape in one paragraph: **work items are issues, available for work; any
19	number of executors pull from them.** A thin generator tick gives every
20	recurring task a standing work item at its anchor and flips blocked items
21	ready — pure label mechanics, no preconditions, no signals. An executor — a
22	GitHub Action by default, but anything that can read issues — picks up the
23	next ready item, claims it by label, evaluates the precondition (the only
24	place it ever runs): on a go it runs prework and hands off to agentic work (a
25	CCR session invoked by API); on a no-go the item **rolls** — stamped
26	not-before the task's next anchor, blocked, reason recorded — so the item
27	itself carries "asked, declined, wakes at T". Follow-ups, fan-outs, urgency,
28	and one-off forcing are all just *creating or waking work items*. There is no
29	slot id, no run-ledger watermark, no exclusive claim, and no label-event
30	re-arm.
31	
32	---
33	
34	## 1. What the slot machinery costs today
35	
36	The current design is push-shaped: one hourly scheduler run decides, at a single
37	instant, everything that will happen — which tasks are due, whether they run,
38	what they may touch — and encodes the decision into dispatch issues that a
39	label-event-triggered session then executes. Every complication below is a
40	consequence of that shape.
41	
42	- **The slot id is state smuggled into a title token.** `d2026-08-12`,
43	  `h2026-08-12T14Z`, `m2026-08` exist so that a scheduled occurrence has an
44	  identity — which the exactly-once guard needs (title search per slot), the
45	  stale backstop needs (the *leading character* of the slot id is parsed back
46	  into a period, `SLOT_PERIOD_MS`), and forcing needs (the `~f<runId>` marker
47	  appended so an operator re-run of an already-run slot isn't silently
48	  swallowed). Three mechanisms each decode a fragment of scheduler state out of
49	  a string in an issue title.
50	
51	- **Due-ness lives in a platform side channel.** "Has this slot run?" is
52	  answered by the Actions run ledger of the scheduler workflow itself
53	  (`lastSuccessTime`) — a watermark that is not visible beside the work, must
54	  exclude forced runs to stay correct, and whose unreadability has to fail the
55	  whole run (an exit-0 abort would advance it past slots it never evaluated).
56	  The state the system actually cares about — *was this occurrence's work
57	  created?* — is derivable from the issues themselves, and nothing reads it
58	  from there. *(A first cut of the go/no-go ruling briefly reintroduced a
59	  ledger read; the standing-item model (§5) removed it again — the tick is
60	  now a pure function of the clock and the issue list.)*
61	
62	- **A decision made at one instant cannot express ordering, only simultaneity.**
63	  The nightly chain's ordering is faked by anchor-hour staggering, which
64	  collapses whenever GitHub fires the cron late — hence the `exclusive: true`
65	  claim, a task-level hack whose cost is real: **a deferred slot is spent, not
66	  queued**, so a claim on the wrong night silently halves throughput. The
67	  system has no way to say "run B after A"; it can only say "run A alone".
68	
69	- **Label-event invocation is lossy, and the loss shaped three mechanisms.**
70	  The executor routine fires only on a fresh `labeled` event; a lost delivery
71	  leaves an armed issue sitting forever. So: the janitor's re-arm
72	  (remove/re-add the label to emit a new event), the 20-minute grace window so
73	  a re-arm never hands a live session a rival, and the stale escalation that
74	  bounds the re-arm loop. The claim protocol then has to survive *duplicate*
75	  events (the read-swap-confirm lease). All of it is compensation for a trigger
76	  that neither confirms delivery nor can be polled.
77	
78	- **Capacity, urgency, and follow-ups have no home.** There is exactly one
79	  implicit executor per repo and no way to add another; nothing distinguishes
80	  urgent work from routine work; a task cannot schedule a successor ("validate
81	  in two days what tonight's run delivered") except by hoping a future
82	  precondition rediscovers the situation. Forcing (`FORCE_TASKS`) is a special
83	  engine path with its own exemptions (skips preconditions, exempt from
84	  deferral, excluded from the watermark, slot-id marker) — where "run this now"
85	  ought to be the system's most ordinary operation.
86	
87	- **Visibility is split three ways.** Whether something *will* run is ledger
88	  math nobody can see; whether it *is* running is labels on an issue; what it
89	  *did* is a record line in a captured transcript. There is no one place where
90	  the state of the repo's recurring work can be read.
91	
92	What is worth keeping — and this design keeps all of it — is everything the
93	incidents taught: one session executes exactly one item and never sweeps the
94	queue (the duplicate-execution bug, DESIGN §5), the claim is a verified lease,
95	the issue is data and never instructions, behavior-defining content comes only
96	from tracked files, every exit converges to one visible terminal state, and
97	recovery lives in one place, in code.
98	
99	## 2. The shape — a pull-based queue of work items
100	
101	Four roles, strictly separated (this refines, rather than replaces, the
102	2026-08-06 three-responsibility split — the scheduler's job splits in two and
103	shrinks):
104	
105	1. **The generator** — a thin scheduled tick (the repo's one cron, unchanged
106	   rule). Three jobs, all deterministic label mechanics over the issue list:
107	   *instantiate* each recurring task's standing item when its time comes,
108	   *ready* blocked items whose dependencies have resolved and whose not-before
109	   has passed, and *reclaim* dead executor claims. It evaluates no
110	   preconditions and collects no signals (§5); it executes nothing.
111	2. **Executors** — any number of pull workers. Each iteration: pick the next
112	   ready item (urgent first), claim it, evaluate the precondition — the only
113	   place it is ever evaluated — then on a go run prework and either finish
114	   (agentless task) or invoke the agentic phase and hand the item to it; on a
115	   no-go, roll a scheduled item to its next anchor (§5). An executor is
116	   platform-agnostic by construction: its whole interface is issue read/write
117	   plus the repo at HEAD. More capacity = more executors.
118	3. **Agents** — CCR sessions, one per handed-off item, invoked by the executor.
119	   An agent executes its one item's task file, verifies its outcome ceiling,
120	   and converges the item to a terminal state.
121	4. **The janitor** — unchanged in role, smaller in scope: dead executor claims,
122	   dead agent claims, stale-item escalation, queue health review. The re-arm
123	   retires (§11).
124	
125	The queue itself is the repo's issues, and under the standing-item model that
126	sentence is complete: everything the system knows — including "this task was
127	asked, declined, and wakes again at T" — is on a work item. No plan file, no
128	watermark, no ledger read. The tick is a pure function of the clock and the
129	issue list; which is what the sketch means by *visibility into state*.
130	
131	## 3. The work item
132	
133	An issue, `[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>` (plus an optional free-form
134	qualifier after the task, for tasks that legitimately have several concurrent
135	items — a fan-out names its target: `[claudinite-work] sheepdog/fleet-baseline
136	member-repo-x`). **The issue number is the identity.** No slot id: an
137	occurrence needs no name beyond the item that embodies it, and everything the
138	slot id encoded is recovered elsewhere — dedup from the family's creation
139	timestamps (§5), staleness from the task's own declared frequency read at HEAD
140	(§11), forcing from the fact that creating an item *is* forcing (§8).
141	
142	Body, machine-first (same parsing discipline as today's dispatch body — the
143	first line is the task path, validated in code before anything trusts it):
144	
145	```
146	.claudinite/shared/packs/basics/tasks/baselining/task.md
147	
148	Not-before: 2026-08-14T04:00Z            # optional — see §9
149	Blocked-by: #812, #813                   # optional — see §9
150	
151	Execute the Claudinite task above.
152	The Context section below is binding scope — do not re-decide it.
153	
154	### Context
155	- <the creating precondition's binding lines, verbatim — unchanged>
156	
157	### Delivered by prework
158	- <written by the executor at hand-off, unchanged shape>
159	```
160	
161	Everything behavior-defining — model, outcome ceiling, worker content, prework
162	command — is still read from the tracked task files at HEAD, never from the
163	issue. A work item whose task the repo no longer carries is closed as obsolete,
164	exactly like today's exit-14.
165	
166	**Origin marker.** Items the generator creates carry `origin:schedule`; items
167	created by hand, by a task, or by a fan-out do not. The generator's dedup
168	guards (§5) count only `origin:schedule` items, so scheduled work and ad-hoc
169	work never suppress each other — a pending follow-up does not silence tomorrow's
170	occurrence, and an urgent hand-created item does not consume it either. A task
171	whose precondition should care about open follow-ups can see them through the
172	`issues` signal, as task-specific logic where it belongs.
173	
174	## 4. The state machine
175	
176	```
177	                     ┌────────────► closed  outcome:obsolete
178	                     │                    (precondition no longer holds; task gone)
179	 created ─► task:blocked ─► task:ready ─► task:executing ─► task:agent ─► closed  outcome:done
180	            (only when       (queue)       (claimed by an     (handed to        closed  outcome:delivered
181	             Blocked-by /                   executor)          a CCR session)   open    needs-human
182	             Not-before
183	             present)
184	```
185	
186	Labels, the full vocabulary:
187	
188	| label | means | applied by |
189	|---|---|---|
190	| `task:blocked` | waiting on `Blocked-by` issues and/or `Not-before` | creator |
191	| `task:ready` | available for pickup | creator or the tick |
192	| `task:urgent` | modifier: pick before any non-urgent item | creator (write-gated, like every label) |
193	| `task:executing` | an executor holds the claim | executor, on claim |
194	| `task:agent` | an agent session owns it | executor, at hand-off |
195	| `outcome:done` | succeeded; nothing pending (closed) | executor or agent |
196	| `outcome:delivered` | succeeded **and left a live artifact the world still has to act on** — an open PR awaiting review, an armed auto-merge, a store submission (closed; usually paired with a validation follow-up, §9) | executor or agent |
197	| `outcome:obsolete` | never ran: the pickup-time precondition said no, or the task is gone from the repo (closed as not planned) | executor |
198	| `needs-human` | failed, or anomalous — the one triage state (open) | anyone, incl. janitor |
199	
200	This is the sketch's lifecycle with two adjustments, both argued for rather
201	than assumed:
202	
203	- **Executor identity is a claim comment, not a label.** The sketch's
204	  `being-handled-by-executor-1` puts an unbounded set (executor identities) into
205	  a vocabulary that must stay small and queryable; every new executor would mint
206	  a label, and a query for "what is executing" would have to know every
207	  executor's name. One state label (`task:executing`) answers the query; the
208	  claim comment — which the lease protocol requires anyway — carries *who*
209	  (executor id, run URL) and *when*. Same for `task:agent`: the hand-off
210	  comment names the CCR session.
211	- **`succeeded-with-unexpected-result` becomes `outcome:delivered`, and it is
212	  narrower.** "Unexpected" would blur two things that must not blur: a run that
213	  legitimately left a pending artifact within its ceiling (open-pr task → open
214	  PR: *expected*, but the world hasn't finished with it), and a run that
215	  violated its ceiling (a `none` task that opened a PR) — the latter stays a
216	  **failure** converging to `needs-human`, exactly as today's `verify-outcome`
217	  enforces. `delivered` marks the first case only, and is the natural anchor
218	  for a validation follow-up.
219	
220	Terminal-state discipline is unchanged: every item converges exactly once to
221	exactly one of the four ends, with one comment saying what happened.
222	
223	**Label writes are granular, always** ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2): add and
224	remove named labels (REST POST/DELETE), never write the label *set* (PUT,
225	GraphQL `updateIssue`) — a set-write replaces from a stale snapshot and
226	clobbers concurrent transitions, a bug class GitHub's own CLI shipped
227	([cli/cli#4861](https://github.com/cli/cli/pull/4861)). With multiple
228	executors and a tick all moving labels, this is a correctness rule, not a
229	style preference.
230	
231	**The road back from `needs-human`** (SCENARIOS S12/S19, F7): a human who has
232	resolved the cause re-queues the item by removing `needs-human` and applying
233	`task:ready` — the sanctioned retry lever, write-gated like every label
234	operation here. The next pickup re-runs the precondition (§6.4), which is what
235	makes the retry safe even when the failed run half-did its work. Alternatively
236	the human closes the item (optionally superseding it with a forced retry,
237	§8); nothing mechanical ever re-queues a `needs-human` item.
238	
239	## 5. The generator — the standing work item
240	
241	**The tick never evaluates a precondition and never collects a signal**
242	(owner model, 2026-08-13). Creation is calendar-only: at a task's anchor, the
243	tick creates its work item *unconditionally* — the precondition speaks later,
244	at pickup, on the executor (§6.4), which is where the original sketch had it
245	all along. What happens on a no-go is the model's whole trick: the item is
246	**not closed** — the executor stamps it `Not-before: <the task's next anchor>`,
247	swaps it back to `task:blocked`, records the reason, and the item **rolls
248	forward**. The next anchor readies it again; the next pick re-asks. One ask
249	per period, exactly — go/no-go preserved — and the memory of "evaluated,
250	declined, ask again at T" is carried **on the item itself**, in the one place
251	this design keeps state.
252	
253	```text
254	tick(now):
255	  if dormant: return                            # before any read, as today
256	
257	  # ---- job 1: instantiate (calendar-only; no preconditions, no signals) ----
258	  for task in discoverTasks():                  # NO ordering requirement — the
259	    if task.frequency == 'manual': continue     # `after` yield is pick-time (§6.1)
260	    A = mostRecentAnchor(task.frequency, config.taskScheduler, now)
261	    family = issues(title == "[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>",
262	                    label "origin:schedule", state ALL)
263	                    # REST issue list, never the search index (S6/F11)
264	    # F16 self-heal first: nothing documents that a REST list from another
265	    # node sees a creation seconds old, so a stale list can let a duplicate
266	    # standing item through. Assume it will happen rather than that it won't:
267	    # close every open family item but the OLDEST, outcome:obsolete, with a
268	    # dedupe comment. Serialized by the tick's concurrency group.
269	    if count(i.state == OPEN for i in family) > 1: closeAllButOldest(family)
270	    if any(i.state == OPEN for i in family):    continue  # the standing item
271	                                                          # already exists
272	    # the occurrence guard has TWO halves (F13, caught by the simulator): an
273	    # item CREATED at-or-after A covers this occurrence — and so does an item
274	    # CLOSED at-or-after A, because a rolled item created in an earlier
275	    # period that ran and closed today consumed today's occurrence. With the
276	    # created_at half alone, the very next tick after such a close creates a
277	    # second item for the same occurrence: a double execution.
278	    if any(i.created_at >= A or i.closed_at >= A for i in family): continue
279	    createIssue(title:  "[claudinite-work] <pack>/<task>",
280	                body:   taskPath,
281	                labels: ["origin:schedule",
282	                         family.isEmpty ? "task:blocked" : "task:ready"])
283	                # a brand-new task's FIRST item is born blocked with
284	                # Not-before = its next anchor — adoption must not fire
285	                # weekly/monthly tasks off-anchor (the old first-run concern)
286	
287	  # ---- job 2: ready whatever is due --------------------------------------
288	  for item in issues(label "task:blocked", state OPEN):   # any origin
289	    {blockedBy, notBefore} = parseBody(item)
290	    if all(issues(blockedBy).state == CLOSED) and now >= notBefore:
291	      swapLabel(item, "task:blocked" -> "task:ready")
292	
293	  # ---- job 3: reclaim dead executor claims (§11) --------------------------
294	  for item in issues(label "task:executing", state OPEN):
295	    if noActivitySince(item, EXECUTING_LEASH): stripToReady(item, comment)
296	```
297	
298	And the roll, executor-side (the full pick flow is §6):
299	
300	```text
301	on pick, verdict = precondition(signals, config):
302	  go     -> proceed (prework, hand-off, converge, CLOSE with an outcome)
303	  no-go  -> item carries origin:schedule?
304	              yes: Not-before = nextAnchor(task.frequency); ready -> blocked;
305	                   record the reason            # the item ROLLS — not an exit
306	              no:  close outcome:obsolete       # an ad-hoc item has no next
307	                                                # anchor to roll to (S17)
308	```
309	
310	**What this dissolves, all at once:**
311	
312	- **The evaluate-once ledger.** No `lastTick`, no Actions-ledger read, no
313	  grace fallback: "was this occurrence evaluated" is answered by the standing
314	  item's own `Not-before`. §1's side-channel complaint is fully satisfied
315	  again — the tick is a pure function of the clock and the issue list.
316	- **The 24-attempts cost (F10).** The tick evaluates nothing; the precondition
317	  runs once per wake, i.e. once per period per task. Signals are collected by
318	  the executor for the one picked task — the tick performs no GitHub reads
319	  beyond the issue list.
320	- **Declined occurrences were invisible in every earlier model** — no-go
321	  meant no item (or a ledger entry nobody sees). Now a quiet task's item shows
322	  its last ask, its reason, and its next wake, on its timeline. This closes
323	  the last gap in the sketch's *visibility into state*.
324	- **Forcing needs no item creation in the common case** (§8): the standing
325	  item exists, so force = wake it — strip `task:blocked`, clear `Not-before`,
326	  optionally add `task:urgent`. The same lever as the human re-queue (§4),
327	  which is no accident.
328	- **F9 (topological creation order) retires unbuilt**: `after` no longer
329	  wires `Blocked-by` at creation — see §6.1/§9 — so the tick's iteration
330	  order stops mattering.
331	
332	**Titles carry no timestamp, and never will** (owner question, answered
333	plainly): every item of a task shares the bare title `[claudinite-work]
334	<pack>/<task>`; successive items are told apart by issue number, which is the
335	identity (§3). The optional qualifier exists only for deliberately concurrent
336	items (fan-out targets). Nothing ever parses a date out of a title — that was
337	the slot grammar, and it stays dead.
338	
339	**The costs, named:**
340	
341	- **The issue list's baseline changes meaning.** A quiet repo used to show
342	  zero open scheduler issues; now it shows one open (blocked) item per
343	  scheduled task, each stating its next wake. That is ~a dozen standing open
344	  issues here — read it as the dashboard it is: the issue list *is* the
345	  scheduler's state, which is what the sketch asked for. Filtering them out
346	  of "real issues" views is one label query (`-label:origin:schedule`).
347	- **Hourly tasks churn their item.** An hourly task that stays no-go rolls
348	  ~24 times a day: two label flips and a body edit per roll, on one issue.
349	  Cheap against API quotas, noisy on that item's timeline; the roll writes no
350	  comment (the `Not-before` bump is the record) so the noise is timeline
351	  events, not comment spam. Named and accepted — one issue absorbs it.
352	- **A long-quiet task's item lives for months.** That is the feature wearing
353	  its cost: the item is the task's standing status line, and its age is
354	  information ("quiet since June"), not staleness — the janitor's stale rule
355	  keys on `task:ready` age, which a properly rolling item never accumulates.
356	
357	**Errored and forced items against the guards** (unchanged in substance from
358	the earlier draft, restated for the new shape):
359	
360	- A **failed run** converges its item open + `needs-human` (a real exit — the
361	  roll is only for no-go verdicts, never for failures). The open item *is*
362	  the backlog guard: no new item until a human closes or re-queues it — one
363	  broken task, one triage item, however long it takes.
364	- A **forced ad-hoc item** (no `origin:schedule`) is invisible to both
365	  guards in both directions, whatever state it ends in — it neither
366	  suppresses nor consumes an occurrence (#749's property, kept).
367	- **Force-of-a-scheduled-task** is now the wake lever, not an item (§8), so
368	  the S15 same-title collision cannot arise from the common force at all; the
369	  pick mutex (§6.1) still covers a deliberately created concurrent item.

371	## 6. The executor — pick up, claim, prepare, hand off
372	
373	An executor iteration, in code end to end (the reference implementation is a
374	job in the vendored workflow, triggered by `issues: labeled [task:ready]`
375	events for latency **and** by the tick's cron as the poll that makes lost
376	events irrelevant; `workflow_dispatch` for a hand-started drain):
377	
378	1. **Pick**: list open `task:ready` items; order `task:urgent` first, then
379	   oldest-created. Two skip rules, both live reads at pick time:
380	   - **Same-title mutex** (SCENARIOS S15/F6): skip an item whose exact title
381	     (task + qualifier) has another open item in `task:executing` or
382	     `task:agent` — one task, one execution at a time; a fan-out's distinct
383	     qualifiers still parallelize. The skipped item is picked once its twin
384	     converges.
385	   - **The `after` yield** (SCENARIOS S24): skip a scheduled item whose task
386	     declares `after: [T]` while T's standing item is `task:ready`,
387	     `task:executing`, or `task:agent` — yield *while the upstream is live
388	     this cycle*, nothing more. A rolled upstream (blocked until its next
389	     anchor: it declined this cycle) does not block, and neither does one
390	     sitting `needs-human` — a broken upstream must not halt its dependents
391	     indefinitely, the same bound the old exclusive claim drew at three days.
392	     This is deliberately **not** a `Blocked-by` edge: a standing item that
393	     rolls never closes, so wiring `after` as blocked-by-the-item would
394	     starve every dependent of a quiet upstream forever — the one real trap
395	     in the standing-item model, caught in replay (S24).
396	
397	   **The filters are advisory at pick time (F15)**: they read possibly-stale
398	   state, so two executors can pass them simultaneously and claim
399	   *different* items the filters should have serialized — a twin pair, or an
400	   upstream and its dependent. The per-item lease cannot see this (it
401	   protects one item, not one title). So after **winning** a claim, the
402	   executor re-verifies the filters against live state; if a conflicting
403	   item now holds an **earlier** claim (comment order — the same arbiter the
404	   lease trusts), it reverts its own claim to `task:ready` and moves on.
405	   Bounded (one revert per conflict), deterministic (comment order), and
406	   the earlier claim never notices (S32).
407	
408	   Take the first survivor. None → exit quietly.
409	2. **Claim — the verified lease, unchanged in shape** (it earned its keep):
410	   read labels, abandon if `task:ready` is gone or `task:executing` /
411	   `task:agent` / `needs-human` present; swap `task:ready → task:executing` and
412	   post the claim comment (executor id, run URL, UTC time); re-read, earliest
413	   claim comment wins, loser reverts nothing and moves on — it may pick a
414	   *different* item and try again (an executor is code iterating a queue, not a
415	   session sweeping one; the one-session-one-issue rule binds agents, and each
416	   claimed item still gets exactly one agent). Three precisions the
417	   simulator's validation review forced (2026-08-13), each an implicit
418	   assumption made explicit:
419	   - **"Earliest" means lowest comment *id*, never timestamp** — GitHub
420	     comment `created_at` has one-second granularity, so simultaneous claims
421	     tie on time; comment ids are server-assigned and strictly increasing,
422	     a total order the protocol gets for free. Nothing in the lease may
423	     compare runner clocks.
424	   - **The arbiter is episode-scoped (F18)**: earliest claim comment **since
425	     the item last became ready** — the revert/reclaim/re-queue comment is
426	     the episode boundary. Over the item's lifetime, dead claims accumulate
427	     (every reclaim and revert leaves one behind); arbitrating over all of
428	     them makes a *dead* claim outrank every future live claimant, and the
429	     item livelocks through reclaim cycles forever. Caught by the simulator
430	     racing two executors onto a reverted item (S32) — and masked until
431	     then because a single executor beats its own stale claim by id
432	     equality.
433	   - **The label swap is two API calls, not a CAS** — GitHub has no atomic
434	     label swap. That is fine *because* labels are not the arbiter: they are
435	     visibility and the pick filter; the claim comments arbitrate, so a torn
436	     swap can never mint a second owner. What it *can* do — executor dies
437	     between the remove and the add — is leave an open item with **no state
438	     label at all**, invisible to every rule that filters by state. The
439	     janitor gains the repair (§11): an open work item wearing neither a
440	     `task:*` state nor `needs-human` is off the state machine entirely →
441	     `needs-human`, a human's to look at (same posture as a malformed
442	     item).
443	3. **Validate in code**: the body's first line is a legal task path, the file
444	   exists at HEAD, the pack is declared, `task.mjs` parses. Task gone → close,
445	   `outcome:obsolete`, comment. Malformed → `needs-human` (possible forgery, a
446	   human must see it), unchanged from today.
447	4. **Evaluate the precondition — the only place it ever runs** (the sketch's
448	   "evaluates preconditions", now literally once). Creation was calendar-only
449	   (§5), so this is not a re-check of anything — it is *the* verdict, over
450	   signals the executor collects for this one task. On **go**: proceed, with
451	   the verdict's Context written into the body as the agent's binding scope.
452	   On **no-go**: a scheduled item **rolls** — `Not-before` stamped with the
453	   task's next anchor, `task:ready → task:blocked`, the reason recorded — and
454	   an ad-hoc item (no `origin:schedule`, so no anchor to roll to) closes
455	   `outcome:obsolete` with the reason commented (a follow-up whose world
456	   settled on its own, S17). **This amends §12.3's "the precondition is the
457	   only decision point" by re-siting, not weakening it**: still exactly the
458	   precondition deciding, still one decision point — moved from the scheduler
459	   run to the pick — and prework and the agent still may not skip; the
460	   doctrine's target (later phases inventing "new reasons to skip") is
461	   untouched.
462	
463	   **This stays clean only while preconditions ask task questions, not
464	   calendar ones** (owner's condition, 2026-08-13). "Is there work?" is a
465	   question about the world; "has it been more than a day?" is the scheduler's
466	   own question leaking into a task, and under this model it is doubly wrong —
467	   the item already *carries* its schedule in `Not-before`, so a calendar
468	   precondition would be a second clock disagreeing with the first. Timing
469	   belongs to `frequency`, the anchors, and `Not-before`. The rule is
470	   **advisory** by owner ruling: no mechanical check (the property is not
471	   checkable), and the residual exposure is an item rolled with a calendar
472	   reason in its record — visible, and it costs a cycle, not correctness. The one live offender is resolved by
473	   ruling rather than grandfathered: **baselining's `ageDays > 1` gate is
474	   dropped outright** (owner, 2026-08-13: "the wrong precondition"). Its
475	   precondition becomes the work question alone — is the mount behind canon
476	   head, are migration notes unapplied — with cadence carried by
477	   `frequency: daily-2h` and nothing else. The corpus enters the new mechanism
478	   with zero calendar preconditions.
479	5. **Prework**, Action-side, unchanged contract: subprocess, task dir cwd,
480	   `required_secrets` as env, timeout, `CLAUDINITE_REQUEST_AGENT` conditional
481	   hand-off. One requirement now stated explicitly (SCENARIOS S8/F12): prework
482	   must be **re-entrant** — a dead executor's claim is reclaimed and the item
483	   re-picked, so prework can run again over its own half-done work (it already
484	   must survive this today, where a scheduler run dying mid-prework leaves the
485	   slot due; the contract just never said so). Failure → comment +
486	   `needs-human`, `task:executing` removed. Success,
487	   agentless task or no agent requested → converge now: `outcome:done` (or
488	   `outcome:delivered` when prework's payload names a live artifact), close,
489	   done — the quiet-on-success property survives as a *closed* item rather
490	   than no item, which is the better trade: the run is now visible.
491	6. **Hand off**: write `### Delivered by prework` / `### Why the agent is
492	   here` into the body (unchanged shapes), swap `task:executing → task:agent`,
493	   post the hand-off comment carrying a fresh **invocation nonce**, then
494	   **invoke the agent session via the CCR API** with a prompt naming exactly
495	   this issue and that nonce. The nonce exists because API invocation is
496	   **at-least-once under timeout retry** — a call that times out client-side
497	   may still have created a session, and the retry then creates a second
498	   (SCENARIOS S10/F5). The executor cannot distinguish "failed" from
499	   "unconfirmed"; the *agent-side lease* (§7) is what collapses the duplicates.
500	   Invocation failure after in-run retries → **revert** `task:agent →
501	   task:ready` with an attempt-counter comment (`handoff-attempts: N`); each
502	   later pickup retries, the tick cadence its natural backoff, and only at a
503	   bounded attempt count (~5) does the item converge `needs-human` with the
504	   API error quoted — so a transient platform outage costs nothing but delay,
505	   instead of converging every in-flight item to triage (SCENARIOS S9/F3).
506	   Either way a lost hand-off is a *synchronous, visible* event at the
507	   executor, not a silently missing label event (this is what retires the
508	   re-arm — §11, and the credential it costs is §12).
509	
510	An executor run may iterate (claim → … → hand off, next pick) up to a
511	configured `maxItems`; the default is a small number, and each item's claim is
512	independently leased, so executor concurrency is safe at any width. One bound
513	ties the executor to its leash ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2 — the
514	stalled-worker lesson): the executor job's `timeout-minutes` must be **≤ the
515	executing leash**, so a hung runner is killed by the platform before its
516	claim is reaped and re-picked — otherwise a zombie's prework runs beside its
517	replacement's.
518	
519	**Idempotency, honestly (owner concern, 2026-08-13: "I'm not sure we can
520	guarantee all tasks to be idempotent").** Agreed — and the design does not
521	require it. The queue literature's blanket "make handlers idempotent" applies
522	to systems where duplicate *invocations* reach the handler; here every
523	duplicate-invocation path collapses at a lease **before work starts** (the
524	executor claim, §6.2; the agent claim, §7), so what tasks must actually
525	tolerate is much narrower:
526	
527	- **Prework must be re-entrant** — a *sequential* re-run after a
528	  crash-and-reclaim (§6.5). That is convergence ("check what exists, continue
529	  from there"), not idempotency, and it is already required of prework today.
530	  Concurrent overlap with a zombie run is excluded by construction
531	  (`timeout-minutes` ≤ leash, above), not asked of the task.
532	- **Re-executed agent work passes through the precondition again** (§6.4),
533	  and the half-run's artifacts are on the item (Delivered section, the
534	  PR-number comments the agent posts as it works — the item is the run's own
535	  inbox/outbox). A re-pick therefore *sees* what already happened and
536	  converges `outcome:obsolete` instead of redoing it — check-before-act,
537	  carried by the mechanism, not by task-author discipline.
538	- The residual overlap cases are bounded by the **write ceiling**: the worst
539	  historical duplicate produced twin PRs — visible, closeable, never
540	  destructive.
541	
542	And for a task that can promise none of this — a genuinely one-shot side
543	effect (a store submission, an external notification, a payment-shaped
544	action): the contract gains **`on_interrupt: 'requeue' | 'needs-human'`**
545	(default `'requeue'`). Declaring `'needs-human'` makes every recovery path
546	that would re-execute — leash reclaim (§11), hand-off retry (§6.6), the
547	human re-queue lever (§4) — converge to triage instead: **at-most-once plus
548	a human**. This is the ack-early/ack-late dial every queue exposes, and
549	Celery ships ack-early as its *default* precisely so non-idempotent tasks
550	are never silently re-run ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §1); here the safe-side
551	default stays `'requeue'` because most of this fleet's tasks are
552	sweep-shaped, and the one-shot minority declares itself. Running
553	more executors — a second workflow instance, a laptop, a k8s job — requires
554	only an issues-scope token; nothing about the queue knows how many exist.

556	## 7. The agent
557	
558	Today's `executor.md` collapses: the trigger-identification dance
559	(`resolve-dispatch`'s not-mine / scope-mismatch / no-trigger / needs-issue
560	verdicts, the two transports, the no-fallback rule)
561	existed because the session had to *discover* which label event started it. An
562	invoked session is told its item in its prompt — one issue number — and the
563	prompt is written by executor code, not by a human. What survives, verbatim in
564	role: validate the item in code before acting (never trust the prompt more
565	than a label event — re-resolve the task path at HEAD), honor the Context as
566	binding scope, run `task.md` at the declared model with the declared timeout
567	stated plainly, verify the outcome ceiling in code (`verify-outcome`), converge
568	the item (`outcome:done` / `outcome:delivered` / `needs-human` + comment),
569	print the `claudinite-task-exec` record, capture the session. One session, one
570	item, no queue awareness — unchanged, and now structural: the session never
571	receives a queue, only an item.
572	
573	One thing is **added**, not carried over: **the agent claims too**
574	(SCENARIOS S10/F5). Because the executor's invocation is at-least-once (§6.6),
575	two sessions can arrive at one item. So the agent's first act, before any
576	work: post its own claim comment (session id + the invocation nonce from its
577	prompt, which must match the hand-off comment on the item), re-read, and the
578	**earliest agent claim wins** — the loser ends its session without touching
579	the item, exactly the read-swap-confirm shape the executor lease uses. This is
580	the same move the literature makes with single-use task tokens (a second
581	redemption of a Step Functions task token is rejected); GitHub gives us no
582	single-use token, so earliest-claim-wins stands in, as it already does one hop
583	earlier.

585	## 8. Urgency and forcing — creating or waking an item is the whole mechanism
586	
587	- **Urgent** work is an item with `task:urgent`: picked first, and the
588	  `labeled` event gives it executor latency of one spin-up. Nothing else is
589	  special about it.
590	- **Forcing a scheduled task is waking its standing item** (owner model,
591	  2026-08-13). The item exists (§5), so force = strip `task:blocked`, clear
592	  `Not-before`, optionally add `task:urgent` — the same lever as the human
593	  re-queue (§4), which is no accident: "run this now" and "retry this now"
594	  are the same operation on the same object. The executor evaluates the
595	  precondition at pick like always; a no-go rolls the item again with the
596	  reason on record, so a force that finds no work *says so* where the
597	  operator will read it. Truly unconditional force: say so in a Context line
598	  the task's precondition honors — but the default stands that even forced
599	  work is admitted by code. *(Deliberate divergence from #515's "forcing
600	  never consults the task"; its motivating case — the slot gate running
601	  before preconditions made mid-day forcing unreachable — does not exist
602	  here: nothing runs before the pick.)*
603	- **Forcing ad-hoc work is creating an item**: parameterized runs, `manual`
604	  tasks, fan-out targets. The CLI/composite (`create-work-item <pack>/<task>
605	  [--urgent] [--context …] [--supersedes #N]`) writes the generic "forced by
606	  hand — no precondition asserts there is work" Context; `--supersedes`
607	  additionally closes a named errored item as superseded by this retry. The
608	  CLI warns when an open same-title item exists — the pick-time mutex (§6.1)
609	  means the new item queues behind it, and the operator should know they are
610	  queueing, not jumping (SCENARIOS S15/F6). `FORCE_TASKS`, the
611	  forced-verdict path, the `~f` marker and the watermark exclusion all
612	  reduce to these two levers.
613	- **`manual` tasks** are simply tasks the tick never instantiates: their items
614	  are only ever created by hand or by other tasks. The frequency token
615	  survives; the special-case slot resolution for it dies.
616	- **Fan-out across repos** is the enforcer creating one item per member repo
617	  (urgent when the pass is urgent) instead of firing member schedulers with
618	  `FORCE_TASKS` — same write-gated surface, and the fan-in below gives the
619	  enforcer something it never had: a status. Nothing about it is a "fleet
620	  mechanism": it is a task creating items, and if its work needs wider reach
621	  than the repo's ordinary sessions have, it names a wider invocation endpoint
622	  (§12).

624	## 9. Follow-ups, ordering, fan-in — the dependency fields
625	
626	`Blocked-by: #N[, #M…]` and `Not-before: <ISO instant>` on an item, evaluated
627	by the tick (§5). Three patterns fall out, all from the sketch:
628	
629	- **Follow-up validation.** A task whose run delivered something long-running
630	  (a store submission, an armed auto-merge, a real-world change that settles
631	  over days) ends `outcome:delivered` and creates its own follow-up item:
632	  `Blocked-by: #<this item>` (satisfied the moment this item closes) +
633	  `Not-before: <now + settle time>`. The tick readies it when the time passes;
634	  an executor then re-runs its precondition — which checks whether the world
635	  actually settled — and the item either runs, or closes obsolete because
636	  everything landed on its own. The "will anyone check tomorrow?" gap closes
637	  with machinery that is just two body fields.
638	- **Ordering, declared — the exclusive claim retires.** A task may declare
639	  `after: ['basics/baselining']` in `task.mjs`, and it compiles to the
640	  **pick-time yield** (§6.1), *not* to a `Blocked-by` edge: the executor
641	  skips the dependent while the upstream's standing item is live
642	  (ready/executing/agent) this cycle, and picks it the moment the upstream
643	  converges — or rolls. The distinction is load-bearing under the
644	  standing-item model: `Blocked-by` requires the blocker *closed*, and a
645	  standing item that rolls never closes, so wiring `after` as blocked-by
646	  would starve every dependent of a quiet upstream forever (S24 — the one
647	  trap found replaying the model). As a yield: on the late-fire night all
648	  chain items are created together, baselining runs first, extract and
649	  promote follow *the same night* in order; on the routine night where
650	  baselining's precondition declines and its item rolls, extract is pickable
651	  a minute later. Nothing is spent, no task claims a run, and the engine
652	  still never knows what baselining is — `after` names a task id, and the
653	  pick filter reads item states, generically. §12's exclusive-claim
654	  machinery (and its stated throughput cost) deletes. `Blocked-by` remains
655	  the right edge for what it is: dependencies on items that *terminate*
656	  (follow-ups, fan-ins).
657	- **Fan-out with a fan-in.** Fanning out is creating N items (§8). The fan-in
658	  is one more item — the status/aggregation task — created `Blocked-by` all N.
659	  It readies only when every child converged, and its precondition/prework read
660	  the children's outcome labels to report or escalate. "Getting the status of
661	  a fan-out" stops being a bespoke sweep and becomes an ordinary task whose
662	  edges the tick already evaluates.
663	
664	Native GitHub issue dependencies (blocked-by/blocking — GA since Aug 2025,
665	API- and webhook-supported) and sub-issues *mirror* these fields: the tick
666	writes the native edge alongside the body field, buying the dependency UI for
667	free ([RESEARCH](RESEARCH.md) §2). The body fields remain the truth the tick
668	parses — they are portable to any tracker with issues, labels, and comments,
669	which is the platform-agnosticism the sketch asks for. One vendored module owns
670	parse/serialize of the two fields; nothing else touches them.
671	
672	Cycles: the tick readies nothing in a `Blocked-by` cycle, forever, and the
673	stale escalation (§11) surfaces it as `needs-human` after ~2 periods — the
674	same convergence-not-prevention posture as the rest of the system. The tick
675	does not attempt cycle detection; the janitor's health review may.
