677	## 10. Capacity and platform-agnosticism
678	
679	The default deployment stays one vendored workflow — the repo's only cron,
680	rule unchanged — now containing the tick job and one executor job (the tick
681	runs first; the executor drains what it created, which keeps the common case's
682	latency at zero even without events). Event triggers (`task:ready` labeled)
683	give urgent and hand-created items sub-minute pickup. Scaling is a config
684	knob: the executor job's `maxItems`, a matrix width for parallel executor
685	jobs, or executors outside Actions entirely — the executor contract is "issue
686	read/write plus the repo checkout at HEAD", so a runner anywhere with a token
687	qualifies. Executor identity is self-declared in claim comments; the system
688	never enumerates executors, which is why adding one requires telling no one.
689	
690	## 11. Recovery — what the janitor keeps, what dies
691	
692	| failure | today | proposed |
693	|---|---|---|
694	| scheduler/tick miss or late fire | run-ledger catch-up math | same property from the occurrence guard (§5) — the next tick instantiates the most recent occurrence only |
695	| double tick | concurrency group + slot-title search | concurrency group + occurrence-guard search (same window, same answer) |
696	| lost label event | janitor re-arm (remove/re-add), 20-min grace, bounded by stale escalation | **retired** — executors poll on the tick's cron; events are latency sugar, never the only delivery |
697	| duplicate events / racing executors | claim lease on one implicit executor | same lease, N executors — the loser picks a different item |
698	| executor died mid-claim | — (executor was a session; janitor reclaimed via `agent-running`) | **the tick** (owner, 2026-08-13): `task:executing` with no activity past ~1h → strip to `task:ready` with a comment, so a dead executor's item is back in the queue within ~2h rather than ~25h. An executor iteration is minutes, not hours, and a lease checked once a day is not a short lease |
699	| agent session died mid-run | janitor: stale `agent-running` → `needs-human` after ~3h | same, on `task:agent` (a hand-off comment names the session, so the janitor can say *which* session died) |
700	| CCR invocation lost | undetectable (label event fired into the void); surfaced only by re-arm/stale | **synchronous**: the executor sees the API failure, retries, converges `needs-human` with the error (§6.6) |
701	| item never picked up | stale dispatch escalation, period parsed from the slot id's leading char | same escalation, period read from the task's declared `frequency` at HEAD (or a default for ad-hoc items) — no title parsing; the stale item converges `needs-human`, out of the queue |
702	| dependency never resolves | n/a | **the stale-ready rule cannot see it** — a blocked item is never ready (F14, caught by the simulator against S18's claim). The janitor gains a third rule: a blocked item whose blockers have not resolved for ~2 days gets an escalation *comment* — labels untouched, so the item still proceeds by itself the moment its blockers resolve; a human who decides it is dead closes it by hand |
703	
704	The janitor remains an ordinary daily task and shrinks twice over: re-arm and
705	its grace window delete, and the **executing-leash reclaim moves to the tick**
706	— a deterministic label rule, serialized and hourly, which is exactly the
707	tick's kind of work. This amends the 2026-08-06 "all recovery lives in the
708	janitor" split, deliberately: the split's purpose was that recovery happen
709	*once, in one place, in code* rather than in every triggered session, and a
710	rule that runs once per tick satisfies that as fully as one that runs once per
711	day. What stays with the janitor is everything needing judgment or a longer
712	horizon — four rules and a review: the dead *agent* claim (`task:agent`
713	silent past ~3h → `needs-human`, the hand-off comment naming which session
714	died), the stale-ready escalation (unpicked past ~2 periods →
715	`needs-human`), the stuck-dependency sweep (F14 above — comment-only), the
716	stateless-item repair (an open work item wearing neither a `task:*` state
717	nor `needs-human` — a torn label swap's leavings, §6.2 → `needs-human`),
718	and the health review, which gains the queue (ready-item age, blocked-item
719	depth, outcome mix) as its subject and can now compute all of it from
720	issues.
721	
722	Two leash constraints, made explicit by the validation review (2026-08-13):
723	
724	- **The executing leash must exceed every task's prework timeout bound
725	  (F17)** — enforced as a wiring-time conformance check, not a convention.
726	  A prework legally allowed to outlive the leash is reclaimed *alive*, and
727	  the failure is not one duplicate run but a **livelock**: every tenure is
728	  reclaimed before it can finish, prework re-executes each cycle, and the
729	  occurrence never converges (S31's trace). The paired runtime rule: an
730	  executor **re-verifies its own lease at every state transition** (is my
731	  claim still this episode's earliest?) and abandons silently when it is
732	  not — which is what keeps a reclaimed-but-alive runner from handing off
733	  work it no longer owns.
734	- **The agent leash (~3h) assumes agent sessions finish or touch their item
735	  within it** — parity with today's stale `agent-running` sweep, stated as
736	  an assumption rather than discovered as an incident: a legitimately
737	  longer-running agent must comment on its item to reset the activity
738	  clock, or it will be declared dead.
739	
740	Both recovery sites keep the same discipline: **recovery is code, run in one
741	place per rule, never a sweep inside a session that is executing something.**
742	
743	## 12. Invocation is an API call — and the endpoint is a task's to choose
744	
745	**Decided (owner, 2026-08-13): the executor invokes the agent over the CCR
746	API.** This reverses per-project-scheduling §12.6, which declined URL-invoked
747	routines because the label was trigger *and* write-gated authorization, the
748	re-arm was built on it, and an endpoint "would add a callable credential to
749	every repo's Action for no reduction in moving parts". All three premises
750	changed: the authorization surface is unchanged (creating and labeling items
751	is write-gated exactly as labeling was), the re-arm no longer exists to
752	preserve, and the moving parts genuinely reduce — re-arm, grace window,
753	transport-dance exits and the no-fallback doctrine all delete.
754	
755	The cost is accepted, not waved through: **a CCR session-creation credential
756	as an Actions secret in every repo**, readable by anything that can run a
757	workflow with secrets access, blast radius "start agent sessions as the
758	owner". Mitigations, all standard machinery here: a dedicated key scoped to
759	session creation alone, provisioned like any `required_secrets` entry, rotated
760	centrally.
761	
762	**And this is what kills the fleet concept** (owner, 2026-08-13: *"the notion
763	of 'fleet' should be eliminated — a CCR with wider access is just a different
764	API invocation; let specific tasks override the URL and you're done"*). The
765	whole self/fleet apparatus — a second ready label, a second executor routine,
766	`session_scope`, "which dispatches may a repo's executor take" — existed only
767	to keep a broad grant off ordinary sessions while the trigger was a label.
768	Once invocation is a call, reach is a property of *which endpoint you call*,
769	so a task that needs wider access declares a different invocation target and
770	nothing else in the system needs a concept of scope. The canon's curation
771	tasks become ordinary tasks that name a wider endpoint.
772	
773	The declaration shape (owner-confirmed, 2026-08-13): a task declares an
774	endpoint **name**; the repo's config maps that name to the invocation URL and
775	to **the name of the repo Actions secret holding its token**. A raw URL in a
776	`task.mjs` would put deployment detail — and something adjacent to a
777	credential — into a vendored pack file every consuming repo receives verbatim,
778	which is the one thing pack files must never carry; the name keeps the
779	secret-shaped half in the repo's config where `required_secrets` already
780	lives.
781	
782	**The token must be usable from the GitHub Action, and the plumbing is the
783	`required_secrets` plumbing, reused exactly**: the wiring converge stamps each
784	endpoint's secret into the executor workflow's env by name, so the executor
785	job — the *only* place invocation happens — reads it as ordinary environment.
786	This works because Actions secrets are reachable Action-side and nowhere else
787	in a task's life, and Action-side is precisely where the executor runs; the
788	agent session it invokes still carries no secrets, unchanged. Baselining asks
789	the owner (the standing-issue posture) for any endpoint secret the repo
790	declares but has not configured; until then the tasks naming that endpoint
791	converge `needs-human` at hand-off with the missing secret named — the same
792	"nothing fails, the task just doesn't work yet" posture `required_secrets`
793	has.
794	
795	## 13. What retires, what survives
796	
797	Retires: `slots.mjs` (both exports and the slot-id grammar), `lastSuccessTime`
798	and the ledger-read failure mode, `FORCE_TASKS` and `FORCED_VERDICT` and the
799	`~f` marker, the exclusive claim and `deferredByClaim`, the re-arm
800	(`rearmDispatchIssues`) and its grace window, `resolve-dispatch`'s
801	trigger-discovery exits (11/12/13) and the two-transport dance, both
802	`ready-for-agent` labels, `SLOT_PERIOD_MS` title parsing — and, per §12, **the
803	fleet/self distinction entire**: `READY_FLEET_LABEL`, the second executor
804	routine, the deprecated `session_scope` field, and the scope word every
805	executor had to be told and check. Reach is which endpoint a task names.
806	
807	Survives unchanged: the task folder and contract (plus the new optional
808	`after` and `on_interrupt`), preconditions as the only decision point (evaluated at admission and
809	at pickup, §6.4), prework and `required_secrets`, outcome ceilings and
810	`verify-outcome`, the claim lease, one-agent-one-item, terminal convergence,
811	`claudinite-task-exec` records and the usage fold (plus outcome labels as a
812	second, queryable census), the janitor as sole recovery site, dormancy (the
813	tick's first gate, before any read), the issue-is-data security posture, the
814	one-cron rule.
815	
816	## 14. Arrival, updates, secrets — the mechanism's own lifecycle
817	
818	Three flows the design must own beyond steady state: how the mechanism
819	**arrives** in a repo, what happens when the mechanism itself **changes**, and
820	how a task **executes with secrets**. (Owner question, 2026-08-13 — the first
821	two had only S25's fragment until this section; the scenarios named here are
822	executable like the rest.)
823	
824	### Bootstrap — when the mechanism is added
825	
826	The mechanism reaches a repo the way every engine facility does — bootstrap
827	for a fresh repo, baselining's wiring converge for an established one — and
828	its wiring is exactly four things, all idempotent, all from the vendored
829	engine at HEAD:
830	
831	1. **Labels**, create-if-missing: `task:ready/blocked/executing/agent/urgent`,
832	   `origin:schedule`, `needs-human`, the `outcome:*` family.
833	2. **Two vendored workflows**: the tick (cron at the repo's stable hashed
834	   minute, plus `workflow_dispatch` so an operator or a migration never waits
835	   for the cron), and the executor (invoked as the tick's drain job and by
836	   `labeled` events on `task:ready`/`task:urgent`; carries the stamped
837	   secrets env — below).
838	3. **Config**: `taskScheduler.dispatch: "queue"`, the endpoint map (§12), the
839	   anchor schedule.
840	4. **Nothing else** — no seed items, no ledger to initialize. The first tick
841	   after wiring creates every task's first item `task:blocked` until its next
842	   real anchor (§5's first-item rule, S25), so adoption never fires weekly or
843	   monthly work off-anchor on the least-proven repo. The adoption smoke test
844	   is the force lever: wake one item by hand and watch it converge.
845	
846	Pre-existing issues from the slot mechanism (`[claudinite-task]` titles) are
847	invisible to the tick — the family list is title-filtered — so bootstrap into
848	a repo with old-vocabulary issues neither reads nor touches them (S29); they
849	are the old mechanism's to drain or a human's to close.
850	
851	### Updates — when the mechanism changes
852	
853	The mechanism's only durable state is the items, and an item is deliberately
854	schema-thin: a title naming a task, labels naming a state, two body fields,
855	comments as record. Everything else — anchors, guards, yields, leashes,
856	verdicts — is **computed fresh at every tick and pick from the engine and the
857	declarations at HEAD**. That one property decides every update question:
858	
859	- **A task declaration change** (frequency, `after`, precondition, secrets)
860	  applies to its standing item at the item's next evaluation, with no
861	  migration and no relabeling. One precision the simulator pinned (S28): the
862	  stamped `Not-before` is the *one* scheduling fact an item carries, so a
863	  frequency change takes effect **at the wake already stamped** — the item
864	  sleeps out its old wake, is judged there by the new precondition, and the
865	  next roll targets the new anchor. An operator who wants the new cadence
866	  sooner wakes the item — the force lever, as everywhere.
867	- **An engine change** lands through the ordinary update flow (engine release
868	  → members' baselining converges the vendored workflows). In-flight items
869	  survive by construction: a run that claimed an item finishes it on the code
870	  it checked out; every later touch — next tick, next pick, the janitor — is
871	  new code reading labels. The label-and-field vocabulary is the
872	  compatibility surface, nothing else is.
873	- **Which makes grammar changes the one hard case**: renaming a label or body
874	  field strands every open item. Such a change ships with a migration note
875	  (the `migrations/` discipline) that relabels open items, and it is
876	  rehearsed in the simulator first — change `sim.mjs`, and the red tests name
877	  the scenarios the grammar change breaks before any repo runs it. Additive
878	  changes (a new label, a new optional field) need none of this and are the
879	  strongly preferred shape.
880	- **Version skew** inside one run cannot happen (an Actions run checks out
881	  one ref); skew across runs is the in-flight bullet above, and is why every
882	  rule reads state from the item rather than remembering it.
883	
884	### Executing a task with secrets — the whole path
885	
886	GitHub Actions secrets are the only secret store in the system, and the
887	executor workflow is the only consumer. End to end:
888	
889	1. **Declaration** — `task.mjs` lists `required_secrets: ['CHROME_STORE_TOKEN']`:
890	   names only. The declaration is vendored to every consuming repo verbatim,
891	   which is exactly why it must never hold more than a name.
892	2. **Storage** — values live as repo Actions secrets, set once by the owner
893	   in repo settings. Nothing else in the system stores, copies, or logs them.
894	3. **Wiring** — the wiring converge stamps each declared name into the
895	   **executor workflow's env** (`CHROME_STORE_TOKEN:
896	   ${{ secrets.CHROME_STORE_TOKEN }}`). The tick and the janitor workflows
897	   get no secrets — they never execute task code.
898	4. **Execution** — after claim and a go verdict, the executor runs prework as
899	   a subprocess (task dir cwd, timeout) whose env carries exactly the
900	   declared names. **Prework is the only task code that ever sees values.**
901	5. **The agent hop carries nothing** — the hand-off writes body sections and
902	   calls the invocation endpoint with a prompt naming the issue and nonce;
903	   the session works under its own identity. A task whose agent phase needs
904	   a privileged effect routes it through prework's delivered artifact or a
905	   wider invocation endpoint — never a secret in the session.
906	6. **Endpoint tokens ride the same rail** (§12): config maps endpoint name →
907	   URL + the *name* of the Actions secret; the stamp puts it in the executor
908	   env; the executor reads it only at the moment of the API call. The CCR
909	   session-creation token is simply the default endpoint's entry.
910	7. **Missing secret** — declared but not configured: baselining asks the
911	   owner on its standing issue (the adoption-interview posture), and until
912	   set, execution converges the affected item `needs-human` naming the
913	   missing secret — at prework for `required_secrets`, at hand-off for an
914	   endpoint token. Nothing fails silently; the task just doesn't work yet.
915	8. **Rotation** — rotate the value in repo settings; nothing else changes,
916	   because names are the interface everywhere above.
917	
918	Steps 2–3 and 6–8's storage half are Actions-platform behavior the simulator
919	deliberately does not model (prose rows in the coverage map); the
920	needs-human convergence postures are ordinary sim territory.
921	
922	### Migration
923	
924	Deliberately thin here — **the phase plan lives in the tracking issue,
925	[#801](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/issues/801)** (two PRs, two
926	approval points, one same-day validation burst) — with this record keeping
927	only the property that makes it tractable: the two
928	mechanisms coexist per-repo behind `taskScheduler.dispatch:
929	"slots" | "queue"`, sharing the task contract, with disjoint issue families
930	(`[claudinite-task]` vs `[claudinite-work]`) — so the flip is a config edit
931	and the rollback is the same edit backwards, with each mechanism's open
932	items untouched by the other. Every retired slot mechanism deletes in the
933	same PR that lands its replacement's fleet flip. One known migration detail
934	(SCENARIOS F8): the signal collectors' self-trigger exclusions must learn
935	the new vocabulary before the first queue-mode repo flips, or the queue's
936	own items read as repo activity to the preconditions watching it.
937	
938	## 15. Decisions on record (owner, 2026-08-13)
939	
940	The eight questions this design opened, as answered. Where an answer changed
941	the design rather than confirming it, the section it changed is named.
942	
943	1. **Invocation is a CCR API call** (§12). Reverses per-project-scheduling
944	   §12.6; the session-creation credential in every repo is an accepted cost.
945	2. **The precondition re-runs at pickup, and forcing loses its exemption**
946	   (§6.4) — conditioned on preconditions asking task questions, not calendar
947	   ones. #515's rationale does not survive the pull model.
948	3. **Timing in a precondition is advisory, not forbidden** (§6.4): permitted
949	   where the verdict cannot flip between creation and pickup for scheduling
950	   reasons alone. No check — the property is not mechanically checkable, and
951	   the residual failure is a visible `outcome:obsolete`, not a wrong result.
952	4. **A precondition is go/no-go, never maybe-later** (§5) — *changed the
953	   design twice*. First cut: one verdict per occurrence at the first tick
954	   after the anchor, which required a `lastTick` read from the Actions ledger
955	   — a partial rebuild of the very watermark §1 complains about, called out
956	   as such when the owner asked for a state assessment. Resolved by the
957	   owner's **standing-item model** (decision 13 below): the verdict stays
958	   once-per-period, and the memory moves onto the item itself (`Not-before`
959	   roll), deleting the ledger read entirely. Mid-window firing stays out; a
960	   task wanting finer latency declares a finer `frequency`.
961	5. **The fleet concept is eliminated** (§12, §13) — *changed the design*.
962	   Wider reach is a different invocation endpoint, declared by the task that
963	   needs it. `ready-for-agent-fleet`, the second executor routine, and
964	   `session_scope` all delete. (One elaboration flagged in §12: the task names
965	   an endpoint *key*, with the URL and credential in repo config, so no
966	   vendored pack file carries deployment detail.)
967	6. **The executing-leash reclaim rides the tick** (§11) — *changed the
968	   design*. ~2h to recover a dead executor's item instead of ~25h; the janitor
969	   keeps the judgment sweeps. Amends the 2026-08-06 single-recovery-site split
970	   in siting, not in principle.
971	7. **Namespaced labels, executor identity in claim comments** (§4). As
972	   drafted; the sketch's literals and a label-per-executor are both declined —
973	   the first for queryability, the second because executor identities are an
974	   unbounded set.
975	8. **Dependency readiness is the tick's alone** (§9). No converger poke: one
976	   site evaluates `Blocked-by`/`Not-before`, and ~1h per chain link is within
977	   what nightly work tolerates.
978	
979	Standing entries — no decision needed now:
980	
981	9. **Known limitation (S18):** a fan-in blocked on a stuck child waits for a
982	   human; no quorum or deadline semantics at this scale. The janitor's stale
983	   escalation is the visibility. Revisit only on evidence.
984	10. **Ref-creation CAS claims** — `refs/claudinite/claim/<n>` is the
985	    platform's one true first-writer-wins primitive and would replace the
986	    comment lease outright. Recommendation stands: keep comment leases
987	    (visible on the item, sufficient at this concurrency) unless a real
988	    lost-race incident occurs. Recorded so it is not re-derived.
989	11. **Invocation idempotency key** — if the CCR session-creation API accepts
990	    one, pass §6.6's nonce as it: duplicates then collapse at creation and the
991	    agent-side lease becomes a backstop rather than the mechanism. One
992	    API-docs check at implementation time.
993	12. **The no-go record alternative** — every occurrence creating an item born
994	    closed on a no-go was recorded here as the only ledger-free way to keep
995	    every occurrence on record, priced at ~2,500 closed issues a year.
996	    **Superseded by decision 13**, which achieves both properties (no ledger,
997	    every ask on record) with one *rolling* item per task instead of one
998	    closed item per occurrence.
999	13. **The standing work item** (owner, 2026-08-13) — *the generation model,
1000	    settled*. The tick creates each task's item unconditionally at its anchor
1001	    and evaluates nothing; the precondition runs exactly once per period, at
1002	    pick, on the executor; a no-go **rolls** the item to the task's next
1003	    anchor instead of closing it, so the item carries "asked, declined, wakes
1004	    at T" and the tick is a pure function of the clock and the issue list.
1005	    Forcing a scheduled task becomes waking its standing item. One
1006	    elaboration of the owner's literal proposal, flagged in §9: `after`
1007	    compiles to a pick-time yield, not a `Blocked-by` edge — a rolling item
1008	    never closes, so blocked-by would starve dependents of a quiet upstream
1009	    forever (S24). Titles carry no timestamp; the issue number is the
1010	    identity, as ever.
1011	
1012	---
1013	
1014	## Appendix A — the owner's sketch (2026-08-12, verbatim)
1015	
1016	> Can we think of a mechanism where the work items are available for work, and
1017	> an executor (github action) picks up the next task to process, changes the
1018	> label to "being-handled-by-executor-1", evaluates preconditions, runs
1019	> preprocessing, hands off to agentic work (CCR invocation with API), changes
1020	> the label to "being handled by CCR", and ends.
1021	>
1022	> We can implement "urgent" work by a label to hint the executor.
1023	> This can be platform-agnostic, because it just reads issues.
1024	> The execution loop — the thing that runs this flow again — can be implemented
1025	> in many ways.
1026	> If we want more work capacity — create more executors.
1027	>
1028	> The "force flow" is a simple creation of a task (say urgent).
1029	>
1030	> Fanning out is just creating tasks.
1031	> Getting the status of a fan out is a task that is blocked by all individual
1032	> issues in the projects.
1033	>
1034	> A task that runs daily is created after the daily execution time regularly,
1035	> only if it passes preconditions. When the executor runs it — it can re-run
1036	> preconditions. If it ends without agentic work — change label to "succeeded",
1037	> "succeeded-with-unexpected-result" (open PR etc), "failed-needs-human".
1038	> If there is a follow-up validation (of the agentic work, or for long-running
1039	> real world changes) — we can create an issue blocked by this work (so it
1040	> won't be picked up too soon) and blocked by time "delayed" that will be
1041	> picked up by the scheduler to evaluate the time and preconditions.
1042
